newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban say territorial gains no threat to region.
newsitem.headline: Taleban say territorial gains no threat to region.

text.p: The Taleban on Thursday reassured neighbouring countries that recent gains against the opposition alliance in the north of the country posed no threat to the region but warned against interference in Afghanistan.
A statement from the Foreign Ministry in Kabul said the Taleban had no intention of interfering in the affairs of other countries.

"The Islamic State of Afghanistan...respects all international norms of independence, national sovereignty and territorial integrity. It does not wish to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries."
The prospect of a Taleban victory throughout Afghanistan has worried former Soviet republics to the north of the country.

They fear a huge influx of refugees and the possibility that the Taleban might be tempted to export their militant brand of purist Islam to the shaky new nations of Central Asia, with their predominantly Moslem populations.

The Taleban, who already control most of Afghanistan apart from an area in the north controlled by an opposition alliance, say they have captured two more provinces -- Faryab and Sar-i-Pul -- with the help of a mutinuous commander and his troops.

But an opposition spokesman said on Wednesday Taleban forces had not entered Faryab province and negotiations were continuing to try to persuade the mutinous commander, General Abdul Malik, to rejoin the anti-Taleban alliance led by General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The Taleban frequently accuse other countries of supporting the opposition alliance. They principally accuse Iran, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan of aiding groups fighting the Taleban in the north of the country.

"We expect those countries which have been following the mistaken path of continuing to interfere in Afghanistan's internal affairs, instead of short-term interests, should try for lasting friendship, good neighbourliness and mutual cooperation in the fields of economy, social affairs and culture." said the statement.
The Foreign Ministry statement said peace and a single authority in Afghanistan would benefit all neighbouring countries in terms of trade.

The war in Afghanistan has held up the development of trade between Central Asia and the sub-continent. In particular, plans to build a $2.5-billion gas pipeline between Turkmenistan's gas fields and Pakistan have been stymied by the lack of peace and security.
